newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS-French curve-flattening offers rewards.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS-French curve-flattening offers rewards.

text.p: French debt faces weeks of volatility as markets anticipate a snap French election but investors can profit from curve-flattening trades and by a quick foray into Ecu bonds, strategists said on Monday. While the short end of the curve will come under pressure if the franc weakens, analysts said France's commitment to a single European currency among politicians of all stripes -- and the electorate -- would anchor the market and bring yields back down again soon.

"If we see the French franc heading towards 3.40 per mark we're going to see further pressure in the short end," Phyllis Reed, European bond strategist at BZW in London said. "You end up with a great buying opportunity." The entire French curve has already weakened on speculation President Jacques Chirac will announce a snap election for late May/early June. He has already set in motion the procedure for dissolving the National Assembly by calling the required meetings with political leaders. Ten-year French bond yields are now trading only six basis points below German yields compared with 13 basis points a week ago. The impact has been even more dramatic in the short end with the two-year French/German yeild gap shrinking to 25 basis points from 45 basis points a week ago and three month interest rate Pibor futures diving 38 basis points to 96.31 from Thursday.

The key to the markets' next moves will be the franc, Reed said. With the Franc already weakening to around 3.3718/23 per mark at 1104 GMT from 3.3694/99 late on Friday, there will be speculation overnight money rates may need to be prodded higher to defend any challenge to the franc. Although, the ruling centre-right coalition would likely win an election, its majority would be sharply reduced, increasing the leftward pressure on the government, analysts say. Longer term, markets would suffer from suggestions the Socialists, led by Lionel Jospin, would find it difficult forging ahead with austerity measures required to get France into European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) while the economy was still lagging, analysts said.
"I don't think it's going to be a clear cut campaign," Steve Major, head of bond research at Credit Lyonnais in London, said. "We don't really know much of what the Socialists would want to do."

He said initial indications from the weekend were that the Socialists might push for a softening of the EMU criteria, prioritising employment measures and more political control of the European Central Bank, all policies that could slow down the convergence progress. Major suggested that investors put on two-to-five year curve-flattening trades. He expected the spread to narrow to around 95 basis points over the next week or so from around 105 now.

"This is one of these classic French situations. You get a snap move in the Pibor and then everyone realises it was wrong and the curve will resteepen. I would not be holding it for much more than 10 basis points," he said.

Reed at BZW would go for a longer term play. She expected the two-to-10 year spread to widen out to from around 28 basis points now to around 50 basis points during the campaign, offering a prime opportunity to jump into the market.
"On a six month horizon we would look for that spread to be into single digits and that is going to present a good buying opportunity," she said.
Major said uncertainties over the Socialists' EMU commitment and France's role in the currency were also making the Ecu/French 10-year spread look cheap at around 58 basis points.
The market traditionally reaches resistance at around 60 basis points. "It will attract investor and arbitrage interest," he said targetting 45 basis points on the spread before the election.
He added investors should not look to short France into Germany in the 10-year sector as strong domestic interest insulated this area from short-term volatility.
Reed also saw French 10-year yields pushing to around only 10 basis points over Bunds during any election campaign.
Stephen Hannah, chief economist at IBJ International in London, howerver would avoid the French market altogether.

"Europe in the short-term is going through a number of difficulties. One is the French election. Second is the uncertainties surrounding Italy and its minibudget and thirdly is the politicking surrounding Germany, Italy and France hitting the EMU targets," he said.
